questions.stem_markdown: A 17-year-old says, 'My girlfriend and I are both 17 and have been together for ages, so consent is basically assumed now.' Which response is **most appropriate** in NSW?

options.text: In NSW, sexual intercourse or other sexual acts are lawful from age 16 only when both people freely consent, so being in a relationship does not make consent automatic.
Once both partners are over 16, relationship status replaces the need to think about consent.
Because both partners are still under 18, sexual activity remains unlawful until adulthood.
Consent rules matter for intercourse but not for other sexual acts.
For 16- and 17-year-olds, parental agreement is what makes sexual activity lawful.

questions.explanation_markdown: The Louisa notes state that in NSW the age of consent is 16, and that someone aged 16 or older can legally have sexual intercourse or participate in other sexual acts with another person aged 16 or older **as long as both freely consent**. The best response therefore corrects the misunderstanding that a committed relationship makes consent automatic.

why_others_wrong.B: This contradicts the notes, which still require free consent; being in a relationship is not presented as replacing consent.
why_others_wrong.C: The notes state that the age of consent is 16, not 18.
why_others_wrong.D: The notes explicitly include both sexual intercourse and other sexual acts.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes frame legality around age and free consent, not parental agreement.

key_takeaways: In NSW, the age of consent is 16.
The notes apply this to sexual intercourse and other sexual acts.
Free consent still matters even in an established relationship.

questions.stem_markdown: A 16-year-old with a long-term chronic illness attends transition clinic and says, 'You can skip the sexual-health part. People with conditions like mine do not really get into those risks.' Which response is **most consistent** with the notes?

options.text: Sexual health should still be discussed, because sexuality and intimate relationships are part of adolescent development, and young people with chronic illness may have lower knowledge about sexuality and contraception while still engaging in risk behaviours.
Chronic illness usually delays risk-taking enough that sexual-health discussion can wait until adult care.
Transition visits should focus only on disease self-management unless the young person first discloses intercourse.
Sexual-health discussion is mainly for parents in chronic illness clinics because the medical condition is the main issue.
Only pregnancy or STI complications would justify raising sexual health in this setting.

questions.explanation_markdown: The notes treat becoming comfortable with one's own sexuality and intimate relationships as part of adolescent development. They also state that adolescents with chronic illness are more likely to engage in risk behaviours, and the CAH Bible adds that they may have lower knowledge about sexuality and contraception and do not avoid risk behaviours. That makes continued sexual-health discussion appropriate in transition care rather than something to defer or omit.

why_others_wrong.B: This is the opposite of the notes, which warn that adolescents with chronic illness do not simply avoid risk behaviours.
why_others_wrong.C: The notes do not limit sexual-health discussion to young people who have already disclosed intercourse.
why_others_wrong.D: The adolescent-focused notes support direct review of sexuality and transition issues rather than shifting the topic to parents only.
why_others_wrong.E: The notes support anticipatory sexual-health discussion; it is not restricted to after a complication has occurred.

key_takeaways: Sexuality and intimate relationships are normal developmental tasks in adolescence.
Chronic illness does not remove the need for sexual-health review.
Young people with chronic illness may have lower sexuality and contraception knowledge while still engaging in risk behaviours.

questions.stem_markdown: During an adolescent review, a 14-year-old says, 'Everyone in my year is already doing sexual things, so it does not really matter what I think about it.' Which counselling response is **most appropriate**?

options.text: It is worth exploring what you want, what you think others are doing, and what pressures you feel, because intentions, perceptions, and perceived norms are relevant to risky sexual behaviour.
Those beliefs are not useful to discuss; the key issue is only whether intercourse has already happened.
If peers seem to be doing it, that usually means further prevention counselling will not change anything.
Because this is mainly about peer culture, it sits outside adolescent sexual-health review.
The discussion should focus only on the legal age of consent, not on her expectations or perceived social pressure.

questions.explanation_markdown: The CAH Bible lists intentions, perceptions, and perceived norms among the factors relevant to risky sexual behaviour. Louisa's notes also frame adolescent risk-taking as shaped by developmental and social context. Prevention counselling should therefore explore what the young person believes, expects, and feels pressured by, rather than treating those beliefs as irrelevant.

why_others_wrong.B: This ignores the note-based relevance of intentions, perceptions, and perceived norms.
why_others_wrong.C: The notes support prevention counselling, not therapeutic nihilism based on peer behaviour.
why_others_wrong.D: The notes place sexuality within adolescent assessment and do not exclude peer-influenced concerns from review.
why_others_wrong.E: Age-of-consent discussion can matter, but the notes do not support ignoring beliefs and social expectations during prevention counselling.

key_takeaways: Perceived norms can shape risky sexual behaviour.
Prevention counselling should explore intentions, beliefs, and perceived pressure.
Adolescent sexual-health review is broader than simply confirming whether intercourse has occurred.
